short: FedRAMP is the General Services Administration program that sets one standard way to assess the security of cloud services for federal agencies. Its AI Prioritization Initiative ran from August 2025 to April 2026 and ended with three AI services certified. The program is now moving to FedRAMP 20x.
title: FedRAMP and AI
subtitle: The federal cloud security program, the AI services it prioritized, and the move to FedRAMP 20x
body_html:
FedRAMP, the Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program, is the government wide program that sets a standard approach to assessing the security of cloud services used by federal agencies. It is run by the General Services Administration. For AI it matters in one practical way: an agency can adopt an AI service far more easily once that service is FedRAMP certified. FedRAMP ran an AI Prioritization Initiative from August 2025 to April 2026, and it lists three AI services that received FedRAMP Certification in early 2026.

Which AI services are FedRAMP certified through the AI initiative?

FedRAMP lists three prioritized services, each marked as having received FedRAMP Certification in early 2026.

ServiceProvider
ChatGPT Enterprise and API PlatformOpenAI
Gemini for GovernmentGoogle
Perplexity Enterprise Pro for GovernmentPerplexity AI, Inc.

That list is the output of one initiative, not a list of every AI product an agency may use. The FedRAMP Marketplace is the place to check the status of a specific product.

What did an AI service need to be prioritized?

FedRAMP says the initiative prioritized AI based cloud services that give access to conversational AI engines designed for routine and repeated use by federal workers. A service had to meet all five of these conditions.

  • Enterprise features, including single sign on, SCIM provisioning, role based access control and real time analytics.
  • Guaranteed data separation and protection. Model information from training on customer data does not leave the customer environment without the customer's authorization.
  • Demand from at least five CFO Act agencies, or a specific recommendation from the CIO Council.
  • Availability for government use through the GSA Multiple Award Schedule program.
  • The ability to meet the requirements for a FedRAMP 20x authorization within two months of being accepted.

FedRAMP states that the initiative was completed in April 2026 and is no longer open to new entrants. The second condition is the one worth keeping. It is a plain statement of what a government buyer expects from an AI vendor about training on customer data, and a private buyer can ask for the same.

What is FedRAMP 20x?

It is the replacement for the way FedRAMP has worked for more than a decade. FedRAMP describes 20x as moving assurance away from paperwork and toward evidence. A provider sets its own security goals and measures them continuously, and the results are validated automatically where possible through what the program calls Key Security Indicators. The stated principles are transparency, flexibility, accountability, accuracy and automatic validation.

FedRAMP says the full rules for 20x Certification are finalized for three classes, published as the Consolidated Rules for 2026.

ClassWho it is for, in FedRAMP's wordsStatus
Class ACloud services with mature security and compliance programs that want to enter the federal marketplace, with a small amount of information in advanceAvailable
Class BCommon small scale or light use services that a whole agency is unlikely to rely on for important work. FedRAMP pairs this class with the Low level.Available
Class CCommon enterprise services likely to be used across an entire agency or to provide important government services. FedRAMP pairs this class with the Moderate level.Available
Class DHigh impact servicesTo be piloted in Phase 4, estimated for fiscal year 2027

Can a provider use generative AI to produce its FedRAMP evidence?

Not for the data that matters most. The Consolidated Rules for 2026 define deterministic telemetry as verifiable data collected directly from an authoritative source that represents a factual and reproducible observation of a system, such as its state, configuration or behavior. The definition carries a note written for this moment. It says probabilistic inferences, generative outputs and predictive assessments, such as those produced by generative transformer models, are not a factual record of system state and must not be used to generate deterministic telemetry.

That is a federal program drawing a line in its own rulebook. A model may help a team write, summarize or search. It may not stand in for a measurement. Any organization building automated compliance evidence, in or out of government, can borrow the distinction.

Which FedRAMP terms changed in 2026?

The Consolidated Rules launched on June 24, 2026, and they retire several terms people have used for a decade. FedRAMP says a defined term is part of the rule and must be followed precisely, even where the word is used differently elsewhere.

Term in the 2026 rulesWhat it meansWhat it replaces
FedRAMP CertifiedThe status of a cloud service offering that has received FedRAMP Certification and meets the legal requirement to be FedRAMP authorizedThe program now says Certified where it said Authorized. The statute still uses authorization.
Assessor, and FedRAMP RecognizedAn independent assessment service recognized by FedRAMP to perform assessments. FedRAMP itself is the final assessor.Third Party Assessment Organization, or 3PAO
Security Decision RecordA persistently maintained and validated record of the security decisions a provider makes over the life of an offering, with rationale, resulting customer risk and findingsThe System Security Plan
Certification ProfileThe combination of a type, Rev5 or 20x, a path, Program or Agency, and a class, A through D. The agency path is a legacy path open only to Rev5.No single earlier term
Trust CenterThe secure repository a provider uses to store and share its certification data, and the definitive source for itPackages passed around as documents

FedRAMP describes the two types this way: Rev5 follows a legacy approach based primarily on documented plans, and 20x follows a modern approach based primarily on measured outcomes. The rules are also published in machine readable form in a public repository, which is unusual for a government rulebook and fits the program's own emphasis on automation.

How did FedRAMP get here, and what happens to the old process?

The FedRAMP Authorization Act of December 2022 established the program in law. OMB Memorandum M-24-15, in July 2024, replaced the earlier policy with one built around new authorization paths and automation. GSA announced 20x in March 2025. A Low pilot ran from April to September 2025 and drew 26 complete submissions. A Moderate pilot ran from November 18, 2025 through March 2026, and AI prioritized offerings were among the limited group allowed to take part.

The older process is known as Rev5. FedRAMP says it will stop accepting new Rev5 Certifications on June 11, 2027, and will publish a transition path for services that already hold one. Dates beyond the current phase are given by FedRAMP as estimates, not commitments.

What are the key FedRAMP dates for 2026 and 2027?

These come from the Important Dates page of the Consolidated Rules for 2026. Unlike the phase estimates above, they are the dates written into the rules. Two are still ahead as of September 2026: mandatory adoption on January 1, 2027, and the end of new Rev5 Certifications on June 11, 2027.

DateMilestoneWhat it means
July 4, 2026Optional early adoptionAll stakeholders should begin moving to the Consolidated Rules
July 6, 2026Marketplace listings open for initial implementationProviders in the initial implementation phase can be listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace
July 28, 2026FedRAMP Ready goes legacyNo FedRAMP Ready submissions are accepted after this date. Providers should seek 20x Class A instead.
August 3, 2026Class A pipeline opensFedRAMP begins accepting applications for 20x Class A Certifications
August 10, 2026Temporary Rev5 program pipelines open for Class B and CLimited providers may apply for a Rev5 Class B or C Program Certification without an agency sponsor
August 31, 202620x Class B and C pipeline opensFedRAMP begins accepting applications for 20x Class B and C Certifications
January 1, 2027Mandatory adoptionThe Consolidated Rules take mandatory effect. Over the following year every provider must follow them to keep its certification.
June 11, 2027End of new Rev5 CertificationsFedRAMP stops accepting applications for new Rev5 Certifications

For an AI vendor that wants federal customers, the practical reading is short. The old entry point, FedRAMP Ready, is closed. The new entry point is a 20x Class A Certification, and its pipeline has been open since August 3, 2026.

What does FedRAMP mean if you are not a federal agency?

FedRAMP binds federal agencies and the vendors that sell cloud services to them. It does not apply to a private company. It still shows up in private vendor reviews, because a certification is evidence that a provider has been through an assessment against a published federal standard.

On this site you will see FedRAMP listed beside SOC 2, ISO 27001 and HITRUST on data center facility pages. They are not interchangeable. FedRAMP is the only one of the four that is a government program.

This page is reference material, not procurement or legal advice. FedRAMP is changing quickly in 2026, so check the program's own pages before relying on a date or a class definition.
